claim: Ad libitum FAD levels were highest in the liver, heart, and kidney among key metabolic organs.
source: Among key metabolic organs, ad libitum FAD levels were highest in the liver, heart, and kidney (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by measurements from male WT mice shown in Figure 1a, with statistical analysis showing significantly higher FAD levels in liver, heart, and kidney versus other tissues.

claim: 99% vitamin B2-deficient diet (B2D) reduced liver FAD levels by 70%.
source: We found that 99% B2D was sufficient to reduce liver FAD levels by 70% (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by FAD concentration measurements in fasted liver tissue from mice exposed to B2D versus control diet, shown in Figure 1c.

claim: B2D significantly blunted weight gain in male mice.
source: Moreover, B2D significantly blunted weight gain (Figure 1d and e)
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements over 4 weeks shown in Figure 1d and e, with statistical significance determined by two-way ANOVA.

claim: B2D reduced fat mass in male mice.
source: body composition measurements showed B2D also reduced fat mass (Figure 1f).
evidence: Supported by body composition measurements showing percentage of body mass as fat, presented in Figure 1f.

claim: B2D strongly reduced oxygen consumption in male mice.
source: B2D strongly reduced oxygen consumption (Figure 1g)
evidence: Supported by recorded traces of oxygen consumption (VO2) during CLAMS measurements shown in Figure 1g, with statistical analysis by ANCOVA.

claim: Substrate preference was unchanged by B2D.
source: but substrate preference was unchanged (Figure 1h).
evidence: Supported by respiratory exchange ratio (RER) measurements shown in Figure 1h.

claim: Animals on B2D moved less during nighttime measurements.
source: Animals moved less during nighttime measurements (Figure 1i).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements during dark periods shown in Figure 1i.

claim: B2D-fed mice consumed the same amount of food as controls in absolute terms.
source: In absolute terms, B2D-fed mice consumed the same amount of food as controls (Figure 1j).
evidence: Supported by cumulative food intake measurements shown in Figure 1j.

claim: Female mice exposed to B2D showed reduced body weight gain and locomotory activity with trends toward lower oxygen consumption in the night phase.
source: Female mice exposed to B2D also showed reduced body weight gain and locomotory activity with trends toward lower oxygen consumption in the night phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by metabolic phenotyping data from female mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Reducing riboflavin in the diet by 90% did not impact liver FAD levels nor influence energy balance.
source: In contrast to B2D, reducing riboflavin in the diet by 90% did not impact liver FAD levels nor influence energy balance (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by measurements of liver FAD concentrations and metabolic phenotyping data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Liver FAD displayed circadian accumulation coinciding with the onset of gluconeogenesis (ZT12).
source: We found that liver FAD displayed circadian accumulation (Patel et al., 2012) coinciding with the onset of gluconeogenesis (ZT12) that occurs before the active period for mice (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by measurements of liver FAD and glucose levels across light/dark cycles shown in Figure 2a, with citation to prior work on circadian accumulation.

claim: Re-feeding mice after 16 hr of fasting raised blood glucose levels.
source: Follow-up experiments also demonstrated re-feeding mice after 16 hr of fasting raised blood glucose levels (Figure 2b)
evidence: Supported by blood glucose measurements in fasted and re-fed mice shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Re-feeding mice after 16 hr of fasting depleted liver FAD concentrations.
source: Follow-up experiments also demonstrated re-feeding mice after 16 hr of fasting raised blood glucose levels (Figure 2b), but depleted liver FAD concentrations (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by liver FAD measurements in fasted and re-fed mice shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Blood glucose concentrations were lower in B2D conditions compared with control diets at all times during the pyruvate tolerance test.
source: Consistent with impaired gluconeogenesis from pyruvate, blood glucose concentrations were lower in B2D conditions compared with control diets at all times during the PTT (Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by blood glucose excursion measurements during pyruvate tolerance tests shown in Figure 2d.

claim: B2D suppressed in vivo hepatic basal glucose production in a liver-specific way.
source: In a liver-specific way, B2D suppressed in vivo hepatic basal glucose production inferred from 3H-glucose infusions into fasted mice (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by basal glucose production measurements using radiolabeled glucose infusions shown in Figure 2e.

claim: B2D reduced average basal glucose production rates by more than 50%.
source: Steady-state basal glucose production rates were reached within 1 hr of infusion (Figure 2e') and B2D reduced average rates by more than 50% (Figure 2e").
evidence: Supported by steady-state glucose production rate measurements shown in Figure 2e' and 2e".

claim: Pathways related to fatty acid catabolism and lipid oxidation were strongly repressed in response to B2D.
source: Consistent with known roles of FAD in FAO, pathways related to fatty acid catabolism and lipid oxidation were strongly repressed in response to B2D (Figure 2f).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq coupled with Panther Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Among the B2D-repressed genes annotated to the GO fatty acid catabolism pathway, several encoded flavoproteins whose loss-of-function cause rare organic acidemias, including Sqor and Ivd.
source: Among the B2D-repressed genes annotated to the GO fatty acid catabolism pathway, we noted several encoded flavoproteins whose loss-of-function cause rare organic acidemias, including Sqor (Friederich et al., 2020) and Ivd (Vockley and Ensenauer, 2006).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis and citations to prior work on organic acidemias caused by these genes.

claim: Flavoprotein genes were enriched among B2D-repressed genes.
source: Reflecting a specific impact of riboflavin deficiency, flavoprotein genes were enriched among B2D-repressed genes (Figure 2g) but not B2D-induced genes.
evidence: Supported by volcano plot analysis of flavoprotein gene expression shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Phospholipid (phosphatidylethanolamine [PE], phosphatidylcholine [PC], and lyso-PC) and diacylglycerol (DG) were robustly attenuated in B2D-exposed mice compared to controls.
source: Lipidomics analysis in the liver identified phospholipid (phosphatidylethanolamine [PE], phosphatidylcholine [PC], and lyso-PC) and diacylglycerol (DG) as robustly attenuated (Figure 2h) in B2D-exposed mice compared to controls.
evidence: Supported by lipidomic analysis results shown in Figure 2h.

claim: Hepatic steatosis accompanied B2D effects, presumably due to increased TG.
source: Hepatic steatosis (Figure 2i) also accompanied B2D effects, presumably due to increased TG (Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by Oil-Red-O stained liver sections shown in Figure 2i and triglyceride measurements in source data.

claim: B2D-induced genes consisted of footprints for transcription factor nodes active in NAFLD, including HNF family members and SREBP1.
source: B2D-induced genes consisted of footprints for transcription factor nodes active in NAFLD (Figure 2k), including HNF family members (Xu et al., 2021) and SREBP1 (Shimano et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by HCT intersection analysis shown in Figure 2k and citations to prior work on these transcription factors in NAFLD.

claim: PPARα binding was strongly enriched near promoter regions for 43 out of 121 putative flavoproteins.
source: Analysis of RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data (Lee et al., 2014; Oshida et al., 2015) discovered strongly enriched PPARα binding near promoter regions for 43 out of 121 putative flavoproteins (p=1.19 × 10–11, hypergeometric test)
evidence: Supported by analysis of published RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data with statistical significance determined by hypergeometric test.

claim: Canonical PPARα target genes were found among the genes downregulated by B2D.
source: Using DNA motif analysis, we also found canonical PPARα target genes among the genes downregulated by B2D (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by DNA motif analysis and enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: B2D reduced PPARα-regulated flavoprotein genes.
source: Furthermore, B2D reduced PPARα-regulated flavoprotein genes (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by volcano plot showing expression levels of PPARα-regulated flavoprotein genes in Figure 3b.

claim: Combined B2D and knockdown of Ppara completely abolished body weight gain relative to control diet conditions.
source: Combined B2D and knockdown of Ppara completely abolished body weight gain (Figure 3d and e) and reduced fat mass (Figure 3f) relative to control diet conditions.
evidence: Supported by body weight and body composition measurements in Ppara ΔHep mice shown in Figure 3d, e, and f.

claim: Ppara ΔHep largely recapitulated B2D effects on blood glucose excursion curves during PTTs.
source: We also learned Ppara ΔHep largely recapitulated B2D effects on blood glucose excursion curves during PTTs (Figure 3g and h).
evidence: Supported by pyruvate tolerance test results shown in Figure 3g and h.

claim: FAD levels were lowered to similar extents by Ppara ΔHep or B2D relative to Pparaflox/flox on control diet.
source: Additionally, FAD levels were lowered to similar extents by Ppara ΔHep or B2D relative to Pparaflox/flox on control diet (Figure 3j).
evidence: Supported by FAD concentration measurements in fasted liver shown in Figure 3j.

claim: Lumiflavin reduced PPRE-luciferase activity in the presence of the PPARA agonist WY-14643.
source: We found lumiflavin reduced PPRE-luciferase activity in the presence of the PPARA agonist WY-14643, suggesting intact FAD pools contribute to PPARα transcriptional activity.
evidence: Supported by PPRE-luciferase reporter assay results in HepG2 cells shown in Figure 3l.

claim: Intact FAD pools contribute to PPARα transcriptional activity.
source: We found lumiflavin reduced PPRE-luciferase activity in the presence of the PPARA agonist WY-14643, suggesting intact FAD pools contribute to PPARα transcriptional activity.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that lumiflavin (a riboflavin analog and competitive inhibitor) reduced PPARα transcriptional activity.

claim: Daily gavage with fenofibrate (300 mg/kg) for 2 wk significantly reduced body weight gain under B2D conditions.
source: Daily gavage with fenofibrate (300 mg/kg) for 2 wk while maintaining mice on diet interventions significantly reduced body weight gain under B2D conditions (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements during fenofibrate treatment shown in Figure 4b and c.

claim: Fenofibrate increased blood glucose in both groups of mice far above pre-gavage levels.
source: Fenofibrate increased blood glucose in both groups of mice far above pre-gavage levels (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by overnight fasting blood glucose measurements before and after fenofibrate treatment shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Hepatic steatosis was not detected in B2D mice that received fenofibrate.
source: When liver histology was examined, we did not detect hepatic steatosis in B2D mice that received fenofibrate (Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by H&E-stained liver sections shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The number of flavoprotein genes induced by B2D+ fenofibrate more than doubled when compared to B2D alone.
source: Consistent with restoration of the flavoprotein transcriptome in response to PPARα activation, we found the number of flavoprotein genes induced by B2D+ fenofibrate more than doubled when compared to B2D alone (Figure 4f).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis of flavoprotein gene expression shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Gene footprints enriched by B2D+ fenofibrate and those depleted in clinical NAFLD converged.
source: Using this approach, we found gene footprints enriched by B2D+ fenofibrate and those depleted in clinical NAFLD converged (Figure 4g), including the GABP transcriptional program inactivated in inflammatory liver diseases (Niopek et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by HCT intersection analysis shown in Figure 4g and citation to prior work on GABP.

claim: Pool sizes for deoxysphingolipids that require alanine condensation with palmitoyl-CoA trended higher with B2D.
source: Pool sizes for deoxysphingolipids that require alanine condensation with palmitoyl-CoA trended higher with B2D (Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by sphingolipid measurements by mass spectrometry shown in Figure 5a.

claim: B2D conditions reduced the NAD/NADH ratio in the liver.
source: Consistent with this idea, B2D conditions reduced the NAD/NADH ratio in the liver (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by hepatic NAD/NADH ratio measurements shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Fenofibrate was incapable of reconciling FAD and FMN cofactor pools.
source: Analysis of FAD and FMN (Figure 5c) confirmed fenofibrate was incapable of reconciling cofactor pools
evidence: Supported by FAD and FMN relative abundance measurements by mass spectrometry shown in Figure 5c.

claim: B2D treatments accumulated oxidized coenzyme Q10 and rodent-biased coenzyme Q9.
source: In contrast to the reduced NAD/NADH, we found B2D treatments accumulated oxidized coenzyme Q10 and rodent-biased coenzyme Q9 (Figure 5e)
evidence: Supported by measurements of oxidized and reduced coenzyme Q10 and Q9 by mass spectrometry shown in Figure 5e.

claim: B2D altered the steady-state levels of valine, methionine, phenylalanine, and caused accumulation of short-chain C5 carnitines that reflect incomplete beta-oxidation of fatty acids.
source: B2D altered the steady-state levels of valine, methionine, phenylalanine, and caused accumulation of short-chain C5 carnitines that reflect incomplete beta-oxidation of fatty acids (Figure 6a).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry measurements of carnitines, amino acids, and hydrophilic metabolites shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Complete removal of dietary riboflavin caused metabolite changes in the liver that enriched for organic acidemias and inborn errors of the TCA cycle.
source: Metaboanalyst (Pang et al., 2021) revealed complete removal of dietary riboflavin caused metabolite changes in the liver that enriched for organic acidemias and inborn errors of the TCA cycle (Figure 6b).
evidence: Supported by Metaboanalyst integration analysis shown in Figure 6b and citation to the analysis tool.

claim: B2D caused accumulation of oxidized TCA cycle metabolic intermediates, including fumarate, malate, and 2HG.
source: Moreover, B2D caused accumulation of oxidized TCA cycle metabolic intermediates, including fumarate, malate, and 2HG.
evidence: Supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Pyruvate recovered blood glucose in B2D to pre-gavage control levels.
source: Our phenotyping analysis of fenofibrate suggested alternative carbon sources might supply the substrates to support glucose production during B2D (Figure 4c), including pyruvate, which recovered blood glucose in B2D to pre-gavage control levels (Figure 6d).
evidence: Supported by change in glucose levels 30 min after pyruvate injection shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Gluconeogenic amino acids (serine, glutamate, histidine, alanine) showed selective and unique accumulation in the combined B2D and fenofibrate treatments.
source: In line with this idea, gluconeogenic amino acids (serine, glutamate, histidine, alanine) showed selective and unique accumulation in the combined B2D and fenofibrate treatments (Figure 6a).
evidence: Supported by amino acid measurements shown in Figure 6a.

claim: B2D+ fenofibrate elevated levels of TCA cycle metabolites citrate and aconitate and increased the fumarate to succinate ratio.
source: Similarly, B2D+ fenofibrate elevated levels of TCA cycle metabolites citrate and aconitate and increased the fumarate to succinate ratio.
evidence: Supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 6a.

claim: B2D+ fenofibrate achieved robust GCN2 expression, eIF2α phosphorylation, and higher ATF4 levels relative to any other treatment.
source: In line with this idea, B2D+ fenofibrate achieved robust GCN2 expression, eIF2α phosphorylation, and higher ATF4 levels relative to any other treatment (Figure 6f).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis for ISR proteins shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Mutations occurring in more than 50% of human flavoproteins cause inborn errors of metabolism (IEMs) with heterogeneous clinical presentations frequently characterized by organic acidemia, fasting intolerance, and fatty liver disease.
source: Along these lines, mutations occurring in more than 50% of human flavoproteins cause inborn errors of metabolism (IEMs) with heterogeneous clinical presentations frequently characterized by organic acidemia, fasting intolerance, and fatty liver disease (Balasubramaniam et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on flavoprotein mutations and IEMs.

claim: FAD supports the activity of flavoproteins that enable the electron transport chain (ETC), the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, and fatty acid oxidation (FAO).
source: In particular, FAD supports the activity of flavoproteins that enable the electron transport chain (ETC), the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, and fatty acid oxidation (FAO).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about FAD's role in metabolism.

claim: NAD can activate nuclear receptor co-activators in the liver for gluconeogenesis.
source: NAD can activate nuclear receptor co-activators in the liver for gluconeogenesis (Rodgers et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Synthetic PPARα agonists promote FAO by directing the activity of pathways for balanced lipid metabolism in the liver.
source: Synthetic PPARα agonists promote FAO by directing the activity of pathways for balanced lipid metabolism in the liver, which consequently supported a series of FDA-approved fibrate drugs for the treatment of hypertriglyceridemia (Jackevicius et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work and established knowledge about fibrate drugs.

claim: Dietary riboflavin (vitamin B2) supplies the backbone for all FAD and FMN synthesis.
source: Nutrition impacts FAD availability for the organism and dietary riboflavin (vitamin B2) supplies the backbone for all FAD and FMN synthesis.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about riboflavin metabolism.

claim: Low riboflavin occurs in cancer, HIV, and cardiovascular disease.
source: Low riboflavin also occurs in more broadly observed diseases including cancer (Kabat et al., 2008; Powers, 2005), HIV (Beach et al., 1992; Fouty et al., 1998), and cardiovascular disease (Tzoulaki et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on riboflavin deficiency in various diseases.

claim: Mice require about 4 mg riboflavin/kg diet for normal growth.
source: Based on data reported by Fenton and Cowgill, 1947, mice require about 4 mg riboflavin/kg diet for normal growth.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on riboflavin requirements in mice.

claim: Mouse chow generally contains almost twice the daily riboflavin requirement.
source: However, mouse chow generally contains almost twice the daily riboflavin requirement (Anonymous, 1977).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on mouse chow composition.

claim: Riboflavin turnover rates in rodents are relatively slow at approximately 16 d.
source: Riboflavin turnover rates in rodents are also relatively slow at approximately 16 d (Yang and McCormick, 1967)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on riboflavin turnover.

claim: Energy expenditure is significantly lower among subjects with LC-FAODs compared to the reference population in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.
source: Indeed, energy expenditure is significantly lower among subjects with LC-FAODs compared to the reference population in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (DeLany et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on energy expenditure in LC-FAODs.

claim: Increased reliance upon glycolysis occurs in mitochondrial disease.
source: Increased reliance upon glycolysis occurs in mitochondrial disease (Robinson, 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on mitochondrial disease.

claim: Elevated TCA cycle intermediates, such as fumarate, act to stabilize antioxidant transcription factors and protect against oxidative stress in the liver.
source: Elevated TCA cycle intermediates, such as fumarate, then act to stabilize antioxidant transcription factors and protect against oxidative stress in the liver (Ashrafian et al., 2012) during the stress of IEMs modeled in our study.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on fumarate's role in oxidative stress protection.

claim: The liver dominates mass-specific metabolic rates.
source: The liver dominates mass-specific metabolic rates (Rolfe and Brown, 1997)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on organ-specific metabolic rates.

claim: Deoxysphingolipids become more abundant in NAFLD from incomplete fat oxidation and accrual of toxic intermediates.
source: Our lipidomics also revealed that B2D caused accumulation of deoxysphingolipids, which also become more abundant in NAFLD from incomplete fat oxidation and accrual of toxic intermediates (Gai et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on deoxysphingolipids in NAFLD.

claim: PPARα activation prevents oxidative stress.
source: PPARα activation prevents oxidative stress (Ip et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on PPARα and oxidative stress.

claim: ATF4 regulation becomes altered in human and rodent NAFLD.
source: ATF4 is the principal downstream effector of the ISR, whose regulation becomes altered in human and rodent NAFLD (Puri et al., 2008; Seo et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on ATF4 in NAFLD.

claim: Induction of shared PPARα and ATF4 targets, including Fgf21, may contribute to hepatoprotection from lipotoxic lipid accumulation.
source: However, induction of shared PPARα and ATF4 targets, including Fgf21, may contribute to hepatoprotection from lipotoxic lipid accumulation (Montagner et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work and speculative reasoning about hepatoprotection mechanisms.

claim: There is evidence fibrates generate beneficial effects in IEMs, including improvement of antioxidant defenses and resolution of inflammation.
source: There is evidence fibrates generate beneficial effects in IEMs, including improvement of antioxidant defenses and resolution of inflammation (Seminotti et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on fibrates in IEMs.

claim: The kidney contributes to glucose production during fasting.
source: One important caveat of these experiments is that the kidney also contributes to glucose production during fasting (Joseph et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on renal gluconeogenesis.

claim: PPARα activation overcomes hypoglycemia and fatty liver phenotypes imposed by B2D.
source: These unbiased approaches strengthen the notion that PPARα activation overcomes fatty liver and hypoglycemia phenotypes imposed by B2D.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that fenofibrate (a PPARα agonist) rescued blood glucose levels and resolved hepatic steatosis in B2D mice.

claim: FAD depletion directly affects liver glucose metabolism.
source: These data indicate that FAD depletion directly affects liver glucose metabolism.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that B2D reduced liver-specific basal glucose production in vivo.

claim: PPARα sustains FAD levels in the liver.
source: Altogether, these findings suggest that PPARα sustains FAD levels and requires riboflavin to direct glucogenic responses in the liver.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ppara knockdown reduced liver FAD levels similar to B2D.

claim: PPARα requires riboflavin to direct glucogenic responses in the liver.
source: Altogether, these findings suggest that PPARα sustains FAD levels and requires riboflavin to direct glucogenic responses in the liver.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that B2D and Ppara knockdown both impaired gluconeogenesis and that lumiflavin reduced PPARα transcriptional activity.

claim: PPARα activation precipitates concerted activation of the ISR to overcome fasting intolerance imposed by B2D.
source: Together, our integrated transcription and mass spectrometry analyses favor a model in which PPARα activation precipitates concerted activation of the ISR, which in turn overcomes the fasting intolerance imposed by B2D (Figure 6g).
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that fenofibrate treatment activated ISR markers, increased gluconeogenic amino acids, and rescued blood glucose levels in B2D mice.

claim: B2D causes reduced energy expenditure as an energy conservation function that adapts the animal to survive FAD and FMN depletion.
source: We speculate these FAO disorders rely on conservation responses when the mitochondria are starved of FAD and FMN required for ETC activity. B2D reduces fat stores and slows metabolism for the energy conservation functions that adapt the animal to survive FAD and FMN depletion.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observation that B2D reduced oxygen consumption and body weight gain.

claim: The NAFLD caused by B2D likely reflects a combination of lower hepatic fatty acid oxidation contributing to the accumulation of liver triglycerides and other complex lipid species observed in obesity.
source: The liver dominates mass-specific metabolic rates (Rolfe and Brown, 1997) and, for this reason, the NAFLD caused by B2D likely reflects a combination of lower hepatic fatty acid oxidation contributing to the accumulation of liver triglycerides and other complex lipid species observed in obesity (Shi et al., 2022).
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the observation of hepatic steatosis and reduced fatty acid oxidation gene expression in B2D, combined with citation to prior work.

claim: The stress of B2D gives rise to an environment for fenofibrate and PPARα activation to co-opt the ISR, adapt to TCA cycle dysfunction, and engage hypoxia enzymes to reconcile anaplerosis.
source: Likewise, our data support the idea that the stress of B2D gives rise to an environment for fenofibrate and PPARα activation to co-opt the ISR, adapt to TCA cycle dysfunction, and engage hypoxia enzymes to reconcile anaplerosis.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the combined observations of ISR activation, altered TCA cycle metabolites, and hypoxia gene signatures in B2D+fenofibrate conditions.

claim: Deoxysphingolipids impair mitochondrial function and lead to an energy deficit, especially in the liver, where fasting requires elevated demand for biomass.
source: Notably, deoxysphingolipids impair mitochondrial function (Alecu et al., 2017; Muthusamy et al., 2020) and lead to an energy deficit, especially in the liver, where fasting requires elevated demand for biomass.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on deoxysphingolipids and mitochondrial function, combined with inference about liver energy demands.

claim: B2D restricts mitochondrial function, which causes reductive pressures that likely exacerbate ROS formation in part through proton leak.
source: The energetic requirements of fasting dictate substrate oxidation and electron transport. B2D restricts mitochondrial function, which causes reductive pressures that likely exacerbate ROS formation in part through proton leak.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the observation of reduced NAD/NADH ratio and altered coenzyme Q pools in B2D.

claim: PPARα activation prevents oxidative stress by merging lower NAD/NADH and oxidized Q, which lowers the free energy of electron transport through complexes I and II.
source: PPARα activation prevents oxidative stress (Ip et al., 2004) by merging lower NAD/NADH and oxidized Q, which, in turn, lowers the free energy of electron transport through complexes I and II.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of altered NAD/NADH and coenzyme Q ratios, combined with citation to prior work on PPARα and oxidative stress.
